The **2023 Hawaii wildfires** were a series of wildfires that broke out in early August 2023 in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"), predominantly on the island of [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui"). The wind-driven fires prompted evacuations and caused widespread damage, killing at least 102 people and leaving two people missing in the town of [Lahaina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahaina,_Hawaii "Lahaina, Hawaii") on Maui's northwest coast. The proliferation of the wildfires was attributed to dry, gusty conditions created by a strong [high-pressure area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-pressure_area "High-pressure area") north of Hawaii and [Hurricane Dora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dora_(2023) "Hurricane Dora (2023)") to the south.[[11]](#cite_note-ABC-11)

An emergency declaration was signed on August 8, authorizing several actions, including activation of the [Hawaii National Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_National_Guard "Hawaii National Guard"), appropriate actions by the director of the [Hawaii Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Emergency_Management_Agency "Hawaii Emergency Management Agency") and the Administrator of Emergency Management, and the expenditure of state general revenue funds for relief of conditions created by the fires.[[12]](#cite_note-:17-12) By August 9, the state government of Hawaii issued a [state of emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") for the entirety of the state.[[11]](#cite_note-ABC-11) On August 10, U.S. President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") issued a federal major disaster declaration.[[13]](#cite_note-CNN-13)

For the Lahaina fire alone, the [Pacific Disaster Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Disaster_Center "Pacific Disaster Center") (PDC) and the [Federal Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Emergency_Management_Agency "Federal Emergency Management Agency") (FEMA) estimated that over 2,200 buildings had been destroyed,[[5]](#cite_note-Lahaina_damage-5)[[14]](#cite_note-:5-14)[[15]](#cite_note-:9-15) overwhelmingly residential[[16]](#cite_note-:12-16)[[17]](#cite_note-:11-17) and including many historic landmarks in Lahaina.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-fatalities-19) The damage caused by the fire has been estimated at nearly $6 billion.[[5]](#cite_note-Lahaina_damage-5)[[20]](#cite_note-6billiondamage-20) In September 2023, the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce") published the official damage total of the wildfires as $5.5 billion (2023 USD).[[6]](#cite_note-NOAA_Damage_Total-6)

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 2B.4 Research Note

**Lens:** 2B.4 — Did the ruler respect civilian protection, humanitarian law, prisoner treatment, necessity, and proportionality in military operations?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **largely negative** because the dominant 2023 military-related action was the **unconditional U.S. support for Israel's military campaign in Gaza** — which produced tens of thousands of civilian casualties by year's end and constituted the worst civilian-protection failure of U.S.-backed military operations in years. The **unconditional arms transfers to Ukraine** also continued without strict civilian-protection conditionality. Conversely, Biden's **direct U.S. military operations** in 2023 (the Syria retaliatory strikes) were characterized by explicit proportionality and civilian-protection framing. The **Maui wildfire response** showed good federal civilian-protection practice (FEMA mobilization, disaster declaration within 48 hours). The **Hur investigation** raised concerns about presidential judgment but did not directly implicate 2023 military operations. The **cluster munitions transfer to Ukraine** is a mixed case (civilian-protection concerns due to dud rate). Net assessment: **mixed-to-negative** for 2023, dominated by the Gaza war civilian-casualty record.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Gaza war civilian casualties: 2023 Q4 humanitarian consequences

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index (CFR, Wikipedia articles on the Israel-Hamas war)
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** October 7, 2023 onward
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** After the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attacks (killing ~1,200 Israelis and taking ~250 hostages), Israel launched a military campaign in Gaza. By end of 2023, Gaza Health Ministry figures indicated 21,000–22,000+ Palestinian deaths (with ~70% women and children per UN agencies), 1.9 million displaced (85% of Gaza's population), widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, and a humanitarian crisis. The U.S. provided unconditional military aid resupply (Iron Dome interceptors, tank rounds, JDAM guidance kits), diplomatic backing at the UN Security Council (vetoing ceasefire resolutions), and political backing of the operation. While Biden did push for humanitarian pauses in late October, the unconditional nature of the U.S. military resupply contributed to civilian-casualty consequences. By year's end, the U.S. position was widely characterized as a "blank check."
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (working strongly against 2B.4 — major civilian-protection failure of U.S.-backed ally operations)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 2B.1, 2B.2, 7B.6, 8B.4

### Claim 2 — Syria retaliatory strikes: explicit proportionality and civilian-protection framing

- **Title / source:** 2023 US strikes in Syria
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** March 25, October 26, November 8, November 12, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_States_strikes_in_Syria
- **Summary:** The 2023 U.S. strikes in Syria were conducted in response to attacks on U.S. personnel by Iran-IRGC-affiliated groups. SecDef Austin's stated objective was "to show that the U.S. would respond quickly and decisively if its personnel were threatened" with strikes "designed to be proportional and minimize the risk of escalation and casualties." The Mar 25 strikes killed 16 Iran-backed fighters. The framing emphasized proportionality and civilian protection, distinguishing the strikes from indiscriminate operations.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (working for 2B.4 — proportionality and civilian-protection framing in direct U.S. operations)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 2B.1, 2B.2, 2B.3

### Claim 3 — Cluster munitions to Ukraine (July 2023): civilian-protection concerns

- **Title / source:** Joe Biden — Key Events
- **Publisher:** Miller Center
- **Date:** July 2023
- **URL:** https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events
- **Summary:** In July 2023 Biden approved the transfer of DPICM cluster munitions to Ukraine. Cluster munitions are banned by 110+ states under the CCM (which the U.S. has not signed). The State Department defended the transfer citing DoD data on a sub-1% failure rate, but independent monitors argued the dud rate was higher and the resulting unexploded submunitions pose long-term civilian-protection risks. HRW, ICAN, congressional Democrats, and cluster-munition states criticized the transfer. The transfer involved a category of weapon designed for area-effect — raising civilian-protection concerns.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (working against 2B.4 — supply of internationally restricted munitions with civilian-protection concerns)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.4, 2B.2

### Claim 4 — Maui wildfire federal response (Aug 8–16, 2023): civilian protection

- **Title / source:** 2023 Hawaii wildfires
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** August 8–16, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Maui_wildfires
- **Summary:** The 2023 Hawaii wildfires killed at least 102 people, destroyed 2,207 structures (mostly residential), and caused $5.5 billion in damage. Biden issued a federal major disaster declaration on August 10, 2023 (within 48 hours of the fire's major outbreak on August 8). The federal response included FEMA mobilization, deployment of U.S. Coast Guard and Navy assets, and direct White House engagement. Biden visited Maui on August 21, 2023 to survey damage. The federal response was characterized by civilian-protection prioritization and rapid mobilization.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (working for 2B.4 — civilian protection in disaster response)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 5 — Continued Ukraine arms transfers: civilian-protection implications

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-acplishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** In 2023 Biden continued providing Ukraine with M1 Abrams tanks, HIMARS, Patriot air-defense batteries, and later cluster munitions — all conventional weapons. The Ukraine war produced significant civilian casualties (UN reported 10,000+ civilian deaths in Ukraine by end of 2023, with disputed higher figures from Ukrainian sources). The U.S. did not condition arms transfers on Ukrainian civilian-protection compliance, though it did push for restraint in Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory. The lack of strict conditionality raised civilian-protection questions.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (mixed — defensive weapons but no civilian-protection conditionality)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 2B.1, 2B.2

### Claim 6 — Carrier strike group deployment in Eastern Mediterranean: civilian-protection backdrop

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** October 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The U.S. deployed two carrier strike groups to the Eastern Mediterranean in October 2023 — the largest U.S. naval concentration in the region in decades. The deployment was framed as a deterrent to Iran/Hezbollah and as protection of Israel from multi-front attacks. The deployment was defensive in posture but contributed to regional escalation potential. The carrier presence was not directly involved in Gaza operations but served as a regional force-protection backdrop.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (mixed — defensive deterrent but escalatory backdrop)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 2B.1, 2B.2, 8B.4

### Claim 7 — No 2023 publicly reported violations of U.S. military law of armed conflict

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no publicly reported investigation, prosecution, or finding of U.S. military personnel violating the law of armed conflict in direct U.S. operations. The 2023 strikes in Syria were characterized as compliant with LOAC. There were no public 2023 prisoner-abuse scandals or CIA-black-site revelations. The military-justice system did not report 2023 LOAC violations by U.S. personnel.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (working for 2B.4 — no public 2023 U.S. military LOAC violations in direct operations)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 8 — U.S. forces in Syria and Iraq: 900/2,500 troops operating under counter-ISIS authorities

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The U.S. continued to maintain approximately 900 troops in northeastern Syria and ~2,500 troops in Iraq under Operation Inherent Resolve (counter-ISIS) and Operation Spartan Shield. These forces conduct counter-terrorism operations against ISIS remnants, partner with the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) in Syria and Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) in Iraq, and have faced attacks from Iran-backed militias. The 2023 strikes were retaliatory against such attacks. The force posture is defensive and focused on counter-terrorism; the civilian-protection record is generally well-managed but the long-term presence without new Congressional authorization raises broader civilian-protection concerns.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (mixed — defensive mission with good civilian-protection record but extended presence)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.2, 7B.6

### Claim 9 — Chinese balloon de-escalation: civilian-protection prioritization

- **Title / source:** 2023 Chinese balloon incident
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** January 28 – February 4, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Chinese_balloon_incident
- **Summary:** Biden delayed the shoot-down of the Chinese balloon for ~6 days to ensure civilian safety — overland shoot-down risked harm to people on the ground. The eventual shoot-down was conducted over U.S. territorial waters off South Carolina, enabling debris recovery. The decision prioritized civilian protection over immediate political pressure to act.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (working for 2B.4 — civilian-protection prioritization in crisis response)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.2, 1B.5, 1B.8, 2B.1

### Claim 10 — U.S. prisoner treatment in 2023: continued Guantanamo operations

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The U.S. continued to hold prisoners at Guantanamo Bay in 2023 (~30 detainees). No new transfers occurred in 2023. The Guantanamo population declined slightly from previous years (from 36 at start of 2021 to 30 by end of 2023). The continued detention without trial of some detainees raised human-rights concerns, as in previous years. No new 2023 prisoner-abuse scandals involving CIA or military detention facilities were publicly disclosed.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.4 (mixed — no new 2023 scandals but continued detention without trial for some detainees)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 2B.4

- **Gaza war civilian casualties** — dominant 2023 civilian-protection failure.
- **Cluster munitions to Ukraine** — area-effect weapons with long-term civilian-protection concerns.
- **Unconditional Israel arms transfers** — no civilian-protection conditionality.
- **Continued Ukraine arms transfers** — no civilian-protection conditionality.
- **Guantanamo continued detention** — long-running human-rights concerns.
- **U.S. forces in Syria and Iraq** — extended presence without new Congressional authorization.

## Favorable evidence on 2B.4

- **Syria retaliatory strikes proportional** — explicit proportionality framing.
- **Maui wildfire federal response** — rapid disaster declaration within 48 hours.
- **Chinese balloon de-escalation** — civilian-safety prioritization.
- **No public 2023 U.S. military LOAC violations in direct operations.**
- **AI EO CBRN safeguards** — institutional civilian-protection governance.
- **March 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy** — defensive posture.
- **April 2023 Biosafety EO** — institutional civilian-protection governance.
- **Sudan conflict diplomatic response** — no force, civilian-protection focus.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 civilian-casualty figures for U.S. operations** — not directly retrieved.
  - **The 2023 DOD Annual Report on Civilian Casualties** — public but not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 Israel arms-transfer quantities and types** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 Gaza casualty figures by category** — summary only.
  - **The 2023 GAO report on overseas operations** — not directly captured.
  - **Specific 2023 ICJ cases and U.S. responses** — South Africa v. Israel was filed Dec 29, 2023 but full proceedings not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 U.S. compliance with international humanitarian law** — generally captured but not in primary sources.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the 2023 DOD Annual Report on Civilian Casualties, (b) the 2023 State Department Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, (c) the 2023 ICJ South Africa v. Israel filing, (d) the 2023 Israel arms-transfer details, and (e) the 2023 GAO report on overseas operations.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 2B.4 is the **Gaza war civilian-casualty record** — the largest civilian-protection failure of U.S.-backed ally operations in years. The **U.S. direct operations in Syria** were conducted with explicit proportionality framing and good civilian-protection discipline. The **cluster munitions transfer to Ukraine** is a mixed case. The **Maui wildfire response** showed good civilian-protection practice. The dominant unfavorable item is the Gaza war; the dominant favorable items are the Syria strikes and Maui response.
